title: Money, Banks and Interest
bigQuestion: What does money do for us, and what happens to it when we put it in a bank?

story.title: Ana's Fifty Dollars
story.kicker: Ana puts her birthday money in the bank, and the bank puts it to work.
paragraphs: Ana turned ten, and her grandmother gave her a card with $50 inside. Ana wanted a new art set. But the art set cost $70. She did not have enough yet. "Put it in the bank," her grandmother said. "Let it grow while you wait."

At the bank, a teller named Mr. Ruiz helped Ana open a savings account. Ana handed over her $50. Mr. Ruiz typed it into the computer and gave her a paper slip. It showed $50 in her account. Ana frowned. "Where does my money go now?"

Mr. Ruiz smiled. "Some of it stays here, safe. Some of it we lend to people who need it. A family down the street borrowed money to fix their roof. A baker borrowed money to buy a new oven. They will pay it back, plus a little extra."

"And you get a little extra too," he said. "That is called interest. The bank pays you for letting it use your money." Ana thought about it. Her $50 was helping fix a roof and bake bread. And it would still be hers when she needed it.
story.think: Why would a bank pay Ana to keep her money there? Who else gets helped by her savings?

lessons.title: Trading Without Money
lessons.mainIdea: Barter is trading one thing for another without money, and it only works when both people want what the other has.
reading: Maria has apples. She wants shoes. She walks to the shoemaker and offers 20 apples for a pair of shoes. But the shoemaker says, "I do not want apples. I want milk." Now Maria must find someone who wants apples and has milk.

Trading goods for goods without money is called *barter*. Long ago, many people traded this way. Barter can work. Two friends can swap a sandwich for a bag of chips at lunch. But it only works when each person wants what the other has.

That is the big problem with barter. It is hard to find the right match. It is also hard to split things. How many apples is half a cow worth? *Money* solves these problems. Everyone accepts it, so Maria can sell apples for money and use the money to buy shoes.

words.d: trading goods or services for other goods or services without using money
something people agree to accept in trade for goods and services

look.title: The Lunch Table Swap
look.text: Tyler has a peanut butter sandwich and wants grapes. Nia has grapes but wants cookies. Sam has cookies and wants a peanut butter sandwich. Nobody can make a simple two-person trade.
look.prompt: How could these three friends all get what they want? How would money make it easier?

check.q: What is barter?
choices: Trading goods for goods without money
check.why: Barter means swapping goods or services directly, with no money used.

check.q: Maria has apples and wants shoes. The shoemaker wants milk. What is the problem?
choices: The shoemaker does not want what Maria has
check.why: Barter only works when each person wants what the other has.

check.q: How does money fix the problem with barter?
choices: Everyone accepts it, so you can sell to one person and buy from another
check.why: Because everyone accepts money, you do not need to find a perfect match.

lessons.title: Three Jobs of Money
lessons.mainIdea: Money does three jobs: it helps us trade, it measures what things are worth, and it lets us save.
reading: Think about $5 in your pocket. First, you can trade it for a sandwich. Money used to buy and sell is a *medium of exchange*. Medium means "in the middle." Money sits in the middle of every trade.

Second, money measures value. A book costs $10 and a game costs $30. You can see right away that the game is worth three times as much as the book. Money is a *measure of value*, like a ruler measures length.

Third, money lets you save for later. Apples rot, but a $5 bill still works next month. Money is a *store of value*. You can keep it now and spend it later. Ana saved her $50 because she could not yet buy the $70 art set.

words.d: something people use to buy and sell; money's first job
a way to compare what things are worth; prices in dollars do this
something that keeps its worth so you can save it and use it later

look.title: Adam Smith on Money
look.text: Adam Smith wrote that money became the common tool of trade in every advanced country. With it, people buy, sell and swap all kinds of goods.
look.cite: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776 (Book I, Chapter 4)
look.prompt: Which of the three jobs of money is Smith describing?

check.q: A book costs $10 and a game costs $30. How many times more does the game cost?
check.why: $30 divided by $10 = 3. The game costs 3 times as much.

check.q: Jon keeps $20 in a jar to spend next summer. Which job of money is this?
check.why: Keeping money to use later is money's job as a store of value.

check.q: You pay $3 for a smoothie. Which job is money doing?
check.why: Using money to buy something is its job as a medium of exchange.

lessons.title: Coins, Bills and Bank Accounts
lessons.mainIdea: Money can be coins, paper bills or numbers in a bank account, and all of them can pay for things.
reading: Money comes in more than one form. *Currency* is the coins and paper bills you can hold. In the United States, coins include pennies, nickels, dimes and quarters. Bills include $1, $5, $10, $20, $50 and $100.

Most money today is not coins or bills. It is numbers in a bank account. When Ana put her $50 in the bank, it became a number on the bank's computer. She can take it out as cash or use a debit card to spend it.

A *debit card* takes money straight from your bank account when you buy something. If Ana has $50 and spends $12, her account shows $38. The money is just as real as a paper bill. It is only stored in a different way.

words.d: coins and paper bills that people use as money
a card that takes money straight from your bank account when you pay

look.title: Three Ways to Pay
look.text: At the grocery store, one shopper pays with a $20 bill. The next shopper taps a debit card. The next shopper pays with quarters from a jar. Each one buys a $5 bag of apples.
look.prompt: Did all three shoppers use money? Where did each shopper's money come from?

check.q: Ana has $50 in her account. She uses her debit card to spend $12. How much is left?
check.why: $50 - $12 = $38 left in her account.

check.q: Which of these is currency?
check.why: Currency is the coins and paper bills people use as money.

check.q: Where does a debit card take money from?
check.why: A debit card takes money straight from your own bank account.

lessons.title: Keeping Money Safe
lessons.mainIdea: A bank keeps people's deposits safe, and the government insures bank deposits up to $250,000.
reading: Keeping $500 under a mattress is risky. It could be lost, stolen or burned in a fire. A bank is safer. Money you put into a bank is called a *deposit*. The bank keeps a record of every dollar you put in and take out.

When you put money in, the bank adds it to your account. When you take money out, it is called a *withdrawal*. If Ana deposits $50 and later withdraws $20, her account shows $30. The record helps her keep track.

Bank deposits are also protected. A U.S. government agency called the FDIC insures deposits at member banks up to $250,000. That means if the bank ever failed, the government would make sure savers got their money back, up to that amount.

words.d: money you put into a bank account
money you take out of a bank account
a business that keeps people's money safe and lends money to others

look.title: Ana's Account Record
look.prompt: Add up the rows. How much money is in Ana's account at the end?

check.q: Ana deposits $50, withdraws $20, then deposits $15. How much is in her account?
What is a withdrawal?
choices: Money taken out of a bank account
check.why: A withdrawal is money you take out of your account.

check.q: Why is a bank safer than a mattress for keeping money?
choices: Money grows bigger in a mattress
check.why: The bank records every deposit, and the FDIC insures deposits up to $250,000.

lessons.title: Banks Lend Money
lessons.mainIdea: Banks lend some of the money people deposit to people and businesses who need to borrow.
reading: Ana's bank has many savers. Together they deposit $10,000 this month. Not everyone will take their money out at once. So the bank keeps some cash ready and lends the rest. A baker borrows $3,000 to buy a new oven.

Money that is borrowed and must be paid back is called a *loan*. The person who borrows is a *borrower*. The baker is a borrower. With the new oven, she can bake more bread, hire a helper and earn more money. Then she pays back the loan.

So a bank is a meeting place for savers and borrowers. Savers have money they do not need right now. Borrowers need money now for a house, a car, a business or school. The bank connects them. Money that would sit still gets put to work.

words.d: money that is borrowed and must be paid back
a person or business that takes a loan

look.title: Follow the Money
look.text: Ten families each deposit $1,000 in a small town bank. A farmer comes in and asks to borrow $4,000 to buy seeds and fix a tractor. The bank checks that the farmer can pay the money back.
look.prompt: How much money did the ten families deposit in all? How do both the savers and the farmer benefit?

check.q: Ten families each deposit $1,000. How much did they deposit in all?
A baker borrows $3,000 from the bank. What is the baker?
check.why: The person who takes a loan is a borrower.

check.q: Why can a bank lend out some of the money people deposit?
choices: Savers never want their money back
The bank prints its own money
Not all savers take their money out at the same time
check.why: Banks keep some cash ready and lend the rest, because savers do not all withdraw at once.

lessons.title: Getting Paid to Save
lessons.mainIdea: Interest is extra money a bank pays you for keeping your savings there.
reading: Ana has $100 in a savings account. Suppose the bank pays 5% interest a year. That is an example rate. Percent means "out of 100." So 5% of $100 is $5. After one year, Ana has $100 + $5 = $105.

*Interest* is money paid for the use of money. The bank pays savers interest because it gets to use their money for loans. The rate is written as a *percent*. A higher rate means more money for the saver.
If the bank pays only on the first $100 each year, that is *simple interest*. After two years at 5%, Ana earns $5 + $5 = $10. She would have $110. The longer she saves, the more interest she earns.

words.d: money paid for the use of money; savers earn it and borrowers pay it
a part out of 100; 5% means 5 out of every 100
interest paid only on the first amount saved or borrowed

look.title: Ana's $100 at 5% Simple Interest
look.cite: Made-up example; 5% is an example rate, not a real bank's rate
look.prompt: How much interest does Ana earn each year? How much after 3 years in all?

check.q: Ben saves $200. The bank pays 5% simple interest a year (example rate). How much interest does he earn in one year?
Ana has $100 at 5% simple interest. How much does she have after 3 years?
check.why: She earns $5 each year. 3 x $5 = $15. $100 + $15 = $115.

check.q: Why does a bank pay interest to savers?
choices: It has to give money away
Savers do chores for the bank
It uses their money to make loans
Interest is a kind of tax
check.why: The bank pays savers for letting it use their money to lend to borrowers.

lessons.title: Paying to Borrow
lessons.mainIdea: When you borrow money, you pay it back plus interest, so borrowing costs more than paying cash.
reading: Carlos wants a $200 bike now. He does not have the money. His uncle agrees to lend him $200 at 10% interest for one year. This is an example rate. 10% of $200 is $20. So Carlos must pay back $200 + $20 = $220.

Interest works both ways. Savers earn interest. Borrowers pay interest. The first amount borrowed is called the *principal*. For Carlos, the principal is $200. The interest is the extra $20. Borrowing let him ride now, but the bike really cost $220.

Banks charge borrowers a higher rate than they pay savers. The difference helps the bank pay its workers and stay open. A smart borrower asks two questions. Can I pay this back? Is having it now worth the extra cost?

words.d: the first amount of money saved or borrowed, before interest
money paid for the use of money; savers earn it and borrowers pay it

look.title: Now or Later?
look.text: Carlos can borrow $200 now and pay back $220 in a year (example rate of 10%). Or he can save $20 a month from his allowance and chores and buy the bike with cash in 10 months.
look.prompt: What does Carlos gain by borrowing? What does he give up? Which would you choose, and why?

check.q: Lila borrows $300 at 10% simple interest for one year (example rate). How much must she pay back?
Carlos borrows $200 and pays back $220. What is the principal?
check.why: The principal is the first amount borrowed, which is $200. The $20 is interest.

check.q: Who pays interest?
choices: Savers pay it to the bank
Borrowers pay it to the lender
check.why: Borrowers pay interest for using someone else's money. Savers earn it.

lessons.title: Income, Spending and Saving
lessons.mainIdea: Income is money you get; you can spend it, save it or share it.
reading: Ana gets $10 a week for doing chores. Money that comes in is called *income*. For grown-ups, income is often pay from a job. For kids, it might be an allowance, gift money or money from a lemonade stand.
Once Ana has income, she has choices. She can spend it now on a snack or a comic book. She can save it for the art set. She can share it by giving to a food pantry. Every dollar can go only one way.

So each choice has a cost. If Ana spends $4 on candy, she has $4 less to save. That $4 of saving is what she gave up. When money is limited, deciding where it goes is the most important money skill of all.

words.d: money a person gets, such as pay from a job or an allowance
keeping some income to use later instead of spending it now

look.title: Ana's Choices
look.text: Ana has $10 this week. A comic book costs $4. Her class is collecting money for the food pantry. She is also saving for a $70 art set and already has $50.
look.prompt: How would you split Ana's $10? What does she give up with each choice?

check.q: Which of these is income for a kid?
check.why: Income is money that comes in. Money earned from raking leaves is income.

check.q: Ana has $10. She spends $4 on candy. How much can she still save?
check.why: $10 - $4 = $6 left to save or share.

check.q: Ana needs $20 more for her art set. She saves $5 a week. How many weeks until she has enough?
check.why: $20 divided by $5 a week = 4 weeks.

lessons.title: Making a Budget
lessons.mainIdea: A budget is a plan for how to use your income: how much to spend, save and share.
reading: A *budget* is a plan for your money. You write down your income. Then you decide how much goes to spending, saving and sharing. Ana makes a budget for her $10 allowance. She plans $5 to spend, $3 to save and $2 to share.
Check the math: $5 + $3 + $2 = $10. A good budget uses every dollar of income and not one dollar more. If Ana planned $6 to spend, $3 to save and $2 to share, that adds to $11. She would be $1 short.

A budget helps you reach a *goal*. A goal is something you are saving for. At $3 a week, Ana's goal of $20 more for the art set would take about 7 weeks. If she saves $5 a week instead, she reaches it in 4 weeks. Budgets help you see trade-offs.

words.d: a plan for how to spend, save and share your income
something you plan and save for

look.title: Ana's Weekly Budget
look.prompt: Does Ana's budget add up to her $10 income? What would you change to reach her goal faster?

check.q: Ana plans $5 to spend, $3 to save and $2 to share. What is the total?
check.why: $5 + $3 + $2 = $10, which matches her income.

check.q: Leo's income is $12 a week. He plans $6 to spend and $4 to save. How much is left to share?
Why does a budget help you reach a goal?
choices: It lets you spend more than you have
It shows how much to save each week and how long it will take
check.why: A budget is a plan. It shows how much you save and how soon you reach your goal.

review.q: Why is money easier to use than barter?
review.why: With barter you need a person who wants what you have. Everyone accepts money.

review.q: A shirt costs $15 and a jacket costs $45. Which job of money lets you compare them?
review.why: Prices in dollars measure value, so you can see the jacket costs 3 times as much.

review.q: Sara deposits $80 and withdraws $25. How much is in her account?
What does a bank do with much of the money people deposit?
review.why: Banks keep some cash ready and lend the rest to people and businesses.

review.q: Mia saves $100 at 5% simple interest a year (example rate). How much does she have after 2 years?
Joe borrows $50 and pays back $55. How much interest did he pay?
The FDIC insures bank deposits up to what amount?
review.why: The FDIC insures deposits at member banks up to $250,000.

review.q: Kai's income is $15 a week. He plans $8 to spend, $5 to save and $4 to share. What is wrong?
choices: He planned $2 less than he has
He planned $17, which is $2 more than he has
review.why: $8 + $5 + $4 = $17. That is $2 more than his $15 income.
